canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether an initial unfractionated heparin infusion rate of 14 U/kg/h achieved therapeutic anticoagulation more rapidly than 18 U/kg/h and compared day-1 and day-2 aPTT category distributions.

Eligible patients were veterans aged 18-89 years who received the high-dose weight-adjusted unfractionated heparin protocol at an initial rate of 14 or 18 U/kg/h for at least 12 hours and had at least two aPTT measurements during infusion.

population.label: Eligible hospitalized veterans
inclusion_criteria: At least two aPTT measurements during infusion

canonical_statement: Patients with a documented coagulation disorder, liver failure, or BMI at least 40 kg/m2 were excluded; for patients with multiple qualifying heparin courses, only the first qualifying occurrence was included.

population.label: Study exclusion criteria
exclusion_criteria: Repeat qualifying heparin courses after the first occurrence

canonical_statement: The investigators performed a retrospective chart review at a single Veterans Health Administration facility in the southwestern United States for hospitalizations from January 2009 through August 2011.

The high-dose protocol initial infusion rate was lowered from 18 U/kg/h to 14 U/kg/h after January 2011, so the comparison groups were defined by a protocol change over time rather than randomized concurrent assignment.
The analytic cohort contained 129 patients: 61 started at 14 U/kg/h and 68 started at 18 U/kg/h.
The cohort had mean age 64.4 years (SD 11.7), mean BMI 27.8 kg/m2 (SD 6.3), and only 4 women (3.1%); all women were in the 18 U/kg/h group.

Heparin indications were heterogeneous; the authors counted DVT in 45 patients (35%) and PE in 41 patients (32%), with additional indications including atrial fibrillation/flutter, peripheral vascular disease, artificial heart valve, acute coronary syndrome, intracardiac thrombus, stroke, and others.

The revised high-dose heparin protocol used an initial infusion rate of 14 U/kg/h; the protocol loading dose was 80 U/kg (maximum 8,000 U) with subsequent aPTT-guided boluses, holds, and rate changes.

exposures.details: Initial infusion rate under the revised high-dose protocol; loading dose protocol 80 U/kg, max 8,000 U.

canonical_statement: The prior high-dose heparin protocol used an initial infusion rate of 18 U/kg/h before the January 2011 protocol change, with the same aPTT-guided titration framework shown in Table 1.

exposures.details: Initial infusion rate under the prior high-dose protocol; loading dose protocol 80 U/kg, max 8,000 U.

canonical_statement: Therapeutic aPTT was defined as 58-97 seconds, corresponding at the study facility to an anti-factor Xa concentration of 0.3-0.7 U/mL.

outcome.definition: aPTT 58-97 seconds; corresponds to anti-factor Xa 0.3-0.7 U/mL at the facility.
outcome.measurement_method: aPTT calibrated to facility anti-factor Xa range

canonical_statement: Secondary aPTT outcomes were the day-1 and day-2 morning aPTT values categorized as subtherapeutic, at goal, or supratherapeutic.

concept.text: Morning aPTT category on days 1 and 2

outcome.definition: Categorized as subtherapeutic, at goal, or supratherapeutic relative to the 58-97 second target.

canonical_statement: The primary adjusted analysis used a generalized linear model with gamma distribution and log link for time to therapeutic aPTT, adjusting for age, BMI, and receipt of an initial bolus; gender was not adjusted for because few women were represented.

Categorical outcomes were compared with chi-square or Fisher exact tests, continuous outcomes with Student t tests or Mann-Whitney tests as appropriate, and day-1 versus day-2 marginal aPTT distributions with McNemar tests; alpha was 0.05.
Among 129 patients, 120 (93%) were observed to reach therapeutic aPTT during the study.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that patients starting intravenous unfractionated heparin at 14 U/kg/h reached therapeutic aPTT more rapidly than those starting at 18 U/kg/h under this high-dose protocol.
The authors reported that patients receiving the recommended 18 U/kg/h rate experienced initially elevated aPTT values and suggested potential benefit from a 14 U/kg/h initial rate.
The authors stated that further investigation of lower initial rates versus 18 U/kg/h and rate adjustments for overweight and lower obesity classifications was warranted.
The study was a single-site retrospective chart review in an older, predominantly male veteran population, limiting generalizability to women and to non-VA settings.
The cohort combined acute thrombosis with other indications requiring anticoagulation, which the authors did to increase sample size.
Historical documentation of heparin infusion rates was imperfect and protocol variation was common, so some cases may have been misclassified.

Patients who did not reach therapeutic aPTT were excluded from the generalized linear model; a larger fraction of the 18 U/kg/h group than the 14 U/kg/h group failed to reach therapeutic aPTT (8.8% vs 4.9%), potentially affecting the estimated group effect.
Other patient factors were not collected or had limited representation, and gender was not included in the adjusted model because women were rare in the cohort.
The primary endpoint captured time to first therapeutic aPTT but did not account for subsequent aPTT values that could later be above or below target.
Additional clinical outcomes were limited because the work was conducted as a pharmacy practice residency research project with a constrained completion timeframe.
The study was supported through resources and use of facilities at the Central Texas Veterans Health Care System in Temple, Texas.
The authors declared no financial or other conflicts of interest.
